tip: After dopo che about the future, Italian uses the future perfect: avrete mangiato (will have eaten), not the present.
Entro marks a deadline, meaning by or within a time: entro domani = by tomorrow.
Passive voice uses essere plus a past participle that agrees with the subject: lettera is feminine, so spedita.
After quando about the future, Italian uses the future tense chiuderà (closes), where English keeps the present.
Imparare takes a before an infinitive: imparato a nuotare (learned to swim).
Italian says sotto la pioggia (under the rain) where English says in the rain.
Era strano che triggers the subjunctive: rispondesse is the imperfect subjunctive of rispondere.
Se solo plus the imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish: fosse (were), from essere.
After a superlative like il miglior vino, the relative clause takes the subjunctive: abbia bevuto.
Adverbs like sempre go between the helper and the participle: ha sempre incuriosito, not after it.
Prima che always takes the subjunctive: torni is the subjunctive of tornare.
Bisognava che needs the subjunctive: trovassi is the imperfect subjunctive of trovare.
Dove works as a relative for places, standing in for in cui: la spiaggia dove andiamo.
Reflexive verbs form compound tenses with essere, and the participle agrees: si era addormentata (feminine).
Before the direct object la, the indirect pronoun ti becomes te: te la direi (I'd tell it to you).
Per cui means why or for which after a noun: il motivo per cui (the reason why).
Il quale and its forms replace cui after a preposition: nella quale = in cui (in which).
Unreal if: se plus the imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional: se lavorassi..., avrei (if I worked, I'd have).
Essere d'accordo takes su for the thing agreed on, so the relative is su cui (on which).
Cui placed between an article and a noun means whose: sulla cui cima (on whose top).
Stare plus the gerund makes the -ing present: sto imparando (am learning).
Chi means whoever or he who and always takes a singular verb: chi lavora (whoever works).
